title: A table is not a product

beats.say: Why do people stop trusting the data catalog?
A table is just storage. A data product is data published for others, with everything they need to trust it without asking: an owner, a contract and promises about freshness.
Like a product in a shop, it has a label: what it is, who made it, when it is fresh, and how to complain.
The test: can a new consumer find it, understand it, trust it and use it without a meeting?

check.q: What makes a dataset a data product rather than a table?
opts: An owner, a contract and service levels
It is stored in a lakehouse format
It has more than a million rows
check.why: A product carries what consumers need to trust it: owner, contract, service levels and docs.

work: Pick one table you publish and write its owner and grain.
Ask a consumer what they had to ask you to use it.

title: The parts of a data product

beats.say: What exactly does a data product need?
An owning team with on-call. A purpose and grain. A versioned contract with schema, keys and allowed values. Service levels for freshness and completeness.
Then interfaces to read it, a catalog entry with lineage and examples, access rules for personal data, and a deprecation rule.
Write the contract as a file next to the code, so the platform can check it on every change.

show.title: Contract file

check.q: Where should a data product's contract live?
opts: As a file next to the product's code
In a slide deck for the steering group
In the head of the engineer who wrote it
check.why: A file in the repository can be versioned and checked automatically in CI.

work: Write a contract file for one table you own.
Add two SLOs: freshness and completeness.

title: Breaking changes and versions

beats.say: Can I rename a column in my product?
Removing or renaming a column, changing a type, making a column required, or changing the grain all break consumers.
Adding an optional column or improving freshness does not. Those are minor versions.
A breaking change ships as a new major version beside the old one, with a notice to every reader found in the logs, and a window before the old one is retired.

check.q: A product changes from one row per trip to one row per trip leg. What is it?
opts: A breaking change needing a major version
A minor change because no column changed
Not a change because the name is the same
check.why: The grain changes every count and join, so it is breaking.

work: Add a CI check that diffs your contract versions.
Write your product's deprecation notice period.

title: Products have users: measure them

beats.say: How do you know a data product is worth keeping, or worth the money you spend on it?
Count weekly active consumers, products built on top of it, time to first query for a new reader, and service level attainment.
No readers for ninety days and no dependent products? Announce deprecation, wait the notice period, then archive.
A catalog full of dead tables is why people stop trusting the catalog. Retiring products on evidence is part of the job, not a chore.

check.q: A product has had no readers for 120 days. What should happen?
opts: Announce deprecation, wait, then archive
Delete it at once to save some money
Keep it forever in case it is needed
check.why: Retirement follows the deprecation rule so hidden consumers can speak up.

work: List your products with no readers in 90 days.
Send one deprecation notice this month.

title: Data mesh in one minute

beats.say: The data team's backlog is five months long. What now?
When one central team sits between every source and every consumer, it becomes the bottleneck. Data mesh moves ownership of analytical data to the teams that produce it.
Four principles: domains own their data, data is a product, a self-serve platform makes it easy, and a few global rules are enforced by code.
It is an organisational change, not a tool you can buy.

check.q: What is data mesh, mainly?
opts: A way to organise ownership of data
A database product from one vendor
A faster file format for the lake
check.why: Mesh is an operating model: domains own data products on a shared platform.

work: Measure your data team's backlog in weeks.
Count the domains that produce most of your data.

title: When mesh is the wrong answer

beats.say: Should every company do data mesh?
Skip it when the organisation is small, domains have no engineers, there is no platform, or a better central team would fix the problem.
Often the right answer is partial: keep a central platform and central shared products, and move ownership only to the two or three domains that are ready.
Renaming the warehouse team to the platform team changes nothing. That is mesh-washing.

check.q: When is a full data mesh usually premature?
opts: Nine data engineers and no platform yet
Hundreds of sources and many data teams
Domains with their own data engineers
check.why: A small team without a platform is not yet the bottleneck mesh fixes.

work: Write which of your domains could own data today.
List what your platform would need first.

title: The self-serve platform

beats.say: Why would a domain team bother to own data?
The platform team builds golden paths: a template that creates a product with its contract, tests and CI, plus ingestion, storage, quality checks, a catalog and access rules.
Share storage and the catalog, but isolate compute per domain with quotas, so one domain's backfill does not slow everyone.
Try it: the simulator's shared platform challenge fails until the noisy domain gets its own warehouse.

check.q: One domain's backfill slows every product on the shared warehouse. What is the fix?
opts: Isolate compute per domain with quotas
Ban backfills on the shared platform
Copy all storage into each domain
check.why: Storage and catalog stay shared; compute is isolated per domain.

work: Measure days from new product to first query.
Check whether domains share compute without quotas.

title: Federated governance, in code

beats.say: When many teams own data, how do you stop them from building silos that cannot talk to each other?
A council of domains, platform, security and legal agrees on a short list: owners and contracts before publishing, personal data tagged and masked, shared identifiers, naming, retention.
Each rule is checked by the platform, in CI and on every run. A rule nobody can check automatically is usually theatre.
Everything else, tools, modelling style, internal tables, stays with the domain.

check.q: Which belongs in federated governance?
opts: Every product uses the shared customer_id
Every domain uses the same orchestrator
Every domain names its internal tables alike
check.why: Global rules cover joinability and compliance; tools stay with domains.

work: Write five global rules for your company.
Mark which ones you can check in CI today.

title: Keeping products joinable

beats.say: Three products say customer. Three different numbers.
Products from different domains are only useful together if they share keys and conventions: one customer id issued by its owner, UTC timestamps, currencies with codes.
Fix duplicates by choosing one owner for the concept, publishing a reference product, and renaming the others for what they really are.
Without shared keys and conventions, data mesh gives you something worse than before: well-owned silos that nobody can join.

check.q: Two domains publish customer products with different counts. First step?
opts: Find why they differ, then pick one owner
Average the two counts in a dashboard
Delete the newer of the two products
check.why: Definitions and keys explain the gap; one owner publishes the reference product.

work: Find concepts with more than one product.
Name an owner for each shared identifier.

title: Mesh failure modes

beats.say: Most data mesh programmes that fail do so in the same few ways. Learn them before you start.
No platform, so every domain builds its own stack. Domains without data skills. Duplicate products. Governance theatre.
Cost sprawl, when every domain runs its own clusters all day long. And orphaned products, when a reorganisation leaves nobody owning them.
Each has a fix: platform first, embedded data engineers, shared keys, rules in code, quotas and cost per product, and team ownership.

check.q: Every domain is building its own Kafka and Airflow. What failed?
opts: The self-serve platform was not there first
Domains were given too few owners
The catalog search was too slow
check.why: Without a platform, ownership means every domain builds its own stack.

work: Check your programme against the six failures.
Write one prevention you could start this quarter.

title: Migrating from a central team

beats.say: Leadership wants mesh in eighteen months. Where do you start?
Platform first, used by the central team itself. Contracts on the main sources. Then two or three lighthouse domains with engineers and real consumers.
Dual-run the old central tables and the new domain products, reconcile until they match, move consumers in groups, then retire the old tables.
Report backlog, upstream incidents, time to ship and cost every quarter, and let domains join when they ask to.

check.q: What should happen before the first domain takes ownership?
opts: The platform exists and the central team uses it
Every domain has hired a data team of its own
All 3,000 central tables have been deleted
check.why: Prove the golden path on your own products first, then move ready domains.

work: Pick your lighthouse domains and say why.
Write the four numbers you would report quarterly.

title: Who owns and pays in a mesh

beats.say: In a mesh, who pays for what?
Domains own and fund their products: people, compute and on-call. The platform team owns the golden paths, catalog, policy engine and cost reports.
Shared aggregate products, like company revenue, often stay with a central analytics team. That is fine: the point is a clear owner.
Move off mesh when domains cannot staff ownership, or the platform costs more than the bottleneck it removed.

show.sub: It is a choice, not a creed

check.q: Who should own a company-wide revenue product?
opts: Often a central analytics or finance team
Whichever domain has the most rows
Nobody, because mesh has no centre
check.why: Aggregate products across domains often stay central; what matters is a clear owner.

work: List products that should stay central.
Show cost per product to each owning team.

title: One desk for every question

beats.say: Why does a company with a brilliant data team still wait months for one simple report?

Picture one town clerk who handles every request: permits, taxes, parking. At first, that works. Then the town becomes a city. The clerk has a queue of thousands, and does not understand most of the forms.

Data mesh is the fix. Each department, like payments or trips, looks after its own records and hands them out as a clean, labelled product. A small shared toolkit helps everyone, and a few city rules keep it all compatible.

check.q: What is the main problem data mesh tries to solve?
opts: One central team becomes a bottleneck for data it does not understand
Databases are too slow to answer questions from many departments
Companies store too little data to answer their business questions
Cloud warehouses cannot hold data from hundreds of source systems
check.why: Mesh is an organisational answer to a central team that sits between everyone, with long backlogs and drifting definitions. Storage and speed are not the issue.

work: List the three slowest data requests last quarter and note who waited on whom.
Find one metric that has more than one definition across teams.
Ask which source teams know who consumes their data.

title: The four principles of data mesh

beats.say: What actually changes when you adopt data mesh? Four things, and each one fixes a specific failure.
First, domain ownership. The payments team that runs the payments system also owns its analytical data. Second, data as a product: an owner, a contract, a freshness promise, and real consumers.

chip.text: Source team now cares about breakage

beats.say: Third, a self-serve platform. Instead of thirty teams building thirty stacks, one platform team offers ready-made paths for ingesting, storing, testing and discovering data. Fourth, federated governance: a few global rules on identity, privacy and naming, enforced by code, not by meetings.

check.q: Why does data mesh include a self-serve platform?
opts: So domains do not each build their own full data stack
So the central team can keep modelling every domain
So every domain must use the same business definitions
So governance can be handled through regular review meetings
check.why: Without paved roads, thirty domains would build thirty stacks. The platform removes that duplicated effort so domains can focus on their data.

work: Write down which of the four principles your company already does partly.
List the platform steps a new domain must build alone today.
Pick one global rule, such as a naming standard, that could be enforced in code.

title: Half a mesh fails in predictable ways

beats.say: What goes wrong if you adopt only one or two of the mesh principles?

Ownership without a platform: thirty teams build thirty stacks, and the cost explodes. A platform without product thinking: tables exist, but nobody trusts them because no one owns quality or promises freshness.

Autonomy without governance gives silos. One team keys a customer by user id, another by email, and the two cannot be joined. Also remember, mesh is organisational, not a tool. Buying a catalogue product does not make you a mesh.

check.q: A company gives every domain full autonomy but sets no global rules. What is the likely result?
opts: Data silos that cannot be joined across domains
Faster joins because each domain picks its best key
A central bottleneck that returns through the back door
Lower storage cost because domains share one stack
check.why: Without shared rules on identity and naming, each domain models things differently, so data from different domains cannot be combined.

work: Check whether two domains key the same entity, like customer, in different ways.
Ask who is paged when a published table is stale or wrong.
Avoid calling a catalogue purchase a mesh rollout.

title: When not to build a mesh

beats.say: When is data mesh the wrong answer?

Mesh trades a central bottleneck for coordination cost. Every domain needs engineers who can own data, plus a funded platform team. With forty sources and one team that keeps up, a central warehouse is cheaper and simpler.

Signs you need it: backlog measured in months, definitions that drift, and source changes breaking pipelines unannounced. Even then, start small. Pick two domains, ship a platform path, and set contracts first. Scale the rest once those consumers trust it.

show.title: Adopt it gradually
items: Trigger: months of backlog and drifting definitions
Start with two domains, not twenty
Ship one paved road on the platform

check.q: A company has 40 sources and one central team that keeps up easily. What fits best?
opts: Keep the central warehouse because mesh costs more than it saves
Adopt mesh now because every company will outgrow central teams
Split the team by domain so autonomy is maximised from day one
Replace the warehouse with a data catalogue to fix ownership
check.why: Mesh adds coordination and skill costs in every domain. When one team keeps up, the bottleneck mesh solves does not exist yet.

work: Measure your backlog age and count definition disputes before proposing a mesh.
Choose two pilot domains with willing owners and real consumers.
Budget a platform team before asking domains to own data.

title: Who owns the data? A food court

beats.say: Who gets the phone call at three in the morning when a report is wrong? In many companies, it is a central data team that never made the data.

Picture a food court. Each stall cooks its own food, and if the pizza is cold, the pizza stall fixes it. Domain ownership works the same way. The trips team owns trips data, and it is on call when that data runs late, just like when its app goes down.
Some dishes need many stalls, like one company-wide revenue number. A central finance team can keep those. What matters is one clear owner, not that the central team vanishes.

show.title: One clear owner
items: Stall dishes: owned by the stall
Shared dishes: owned by a central team
Every dish has a named owner

check.q: What is the core idea of domain ownership of data?
opts: The team that produces the data is accountable when it is late or wrong
Every data product must be moved out of the central team permanently
The central team is accountable for any data in the company's warehouse
Each team builds its own tools and the data owner is left unclear
check.why: Ownership means the producing team is accountable and on call for its data, like for its API. Shared products can stay central as long as each has a clear owner.

work: List your five most important tables and write down who is paged when each is late.
Find one dataset where the answer is 'the central team' even though another team creates it.

title: Three kinds of data product

beats.say: If every team owns its data, who owns the number that joins them all?

There are three kinds of data product. Source-aligned products describe what happened, like completed trips, and belong to the trips domain. Consumer-aligned products, like a marketing attribution model, belong to the team that uses them.

Aggregate products join many domains, like company revenue or the executive scorecard. Those often stay with a central analytics or finance team. Owning means three things: engineers inside the domain, a budget, and an on-call rotation. Without all three, ownership is just a name on a wiki page.

check.q: Where does an executive scorecard joining many domains usually live?
opts: With a central analytics or finance team that owns it clearly
With whichever domain produces the largest source table
With every domain jointly and no single named owner
With the platform team that runs the shared infrastructure
check.why: Aggregate products span many domains, so they often stay with a central analytics or finance team. The goal is a clear owner, not removing the central team.

work: Label each of your key data products as source-aligned, consumer-aligned or aggregate.
Check each one has engineers, a budget and an on-call rota behind it.

title: How ownership handoffs fail

beats.say: Why do some data mesh programs end up worse than the central team they replaced?

Because ownership was handed over without the means. If a domain has no engineers who could own data and no budget to hire them, nobody fixes the late table. It just rots, and the old central team gets blamed anyway.

Another trap is no platform. Each domain then builds its own pipelines and storage, and builds them badly, in ten different ways. A third is the rebrand: renaming the warehouse team the platform team changes nothing about who is accountable. Ask what changed in who gets paged.

show.title: Gotchas interviewers probe
items: Rebrand only: same team, same pager

check.q: A warehouse team is renamed the platform team and nothing else changes. What is the result?
opts: Accountability is unchanged, so it is a rebrand and not mesh
Domains now own their data because the new name says so
Mesh is achieved because a platform team exists
Data quality improves as the new name sets expectations
check.why: Mesh changes who is accountable and who is paged. A rename changes neither, so the same bottleneck remains under a new label.

work: Ask of any mesh plan: who is paged, who has budget, who builds the platform?
Spot domains that would own data with zero engineers and flag the gap early.

title: When mesh is the wrong answer

beats.say: When is data mesh the wrong answer? More often than the conference talks admit.
If one data team of under about fifteen people serves a handful of domains, it is not a bottleneck yet. Mesh would add cost and coordination for no gain.
And if the real pain is quality or speed, fix it centrally first. Contracts with source teams, automated tests and an SLO on freshness often solve it at a fraction of the cost.
Mesh is also wrong when domains have no engineers and no budget, or when leadership just wants a rebrand.

check.q: A team of 10 data engineers serves 5 domains, and the pain is late data. What is the best first move?
opts: Add contracts, tests and a freshness SLO with the existing team
Move all datasets to domains and dissolve the central team
Rename the team as a platform team and begin a mesh program
Let each domain build its own pipelines to remove the queue
check.why: A small central team is not yet a bottleneck, and lateness is a quality and speed problem. Contracts, tests and an SLO fix it far more cheaply than a reorganisation.

work: Write a one-page test: team size, domain readiness, platform budget, real pain.
Try central fixes first: contracts, tests and an SLO, then measure.

title: The staff answer: not a full mesh

beats.say: Your CTO asks: should we adopt data mesh? What does a staff engineer say?
Often: not a full mesh. Keep a central platform and a central team for shared products like revenue.
Then move ownership of source-aligned data to just the two or three domains that are ready, meaning they have engineers, budget and appetite for on-call.
Prove it there. Measure late incidents and time to fix. Expand only when the platform and results justify it. This avoids a risky rewrite and keeps one clear owner per product.

check.q: What is the usual staff-level recommendation for a mid-sized company interested in mesh?
opts: Hybrid: central platform and shared products, plus a few ready domains
Full mesh across all domains at once to avoid a long transition
No change ever, since central teams always beat domain ownership
Full mesh but without a platform, to keep costs down at first
check.why: A hybrid keeps a central platform and team for shared products, and moves source-aligned ownership only to domains that are ready, so risk and cost stay low.

work: Pick the two or three most ready domains and write what each would own.
Define success metrics before the pilot: late incidents and time to fix.

title: The ready-made market stall

beats.say: Why would a busy sales team ever bother to run its own data product?

show.text: Why would a team own data?

beats.say: Picture opening a food stall. If you must build a kitchen, wire the power, and chase permits, you will never open. But if the market hands you a ready stall with water, power, a till, and an inspector who visits, you just cook.
A self-serve platform is that market. The platform team builds the ready stall. It is called a golden path: one supported, recommended way to do a common job.
Doing it right becomes the easy option, so people choose it. And the market owner keeps asking one question: how fast can a new stall sell its first meal?

show.title: What good looks like
items: Right way is the easy way

check.q: Why does a platform team build golden paths for domains?
opts: Doing the job the right way becomes easier than doing it badly
Domains are blocked from using any tool outside the platform
Every data job then runs through one central team's queue
The platform team takes over ownership of every data product
check.why: Domains only take ownership if the supported route is the easiest one. The platform enables the domains; it does not block them or take ownership back.

work: List the three jobs your domain teams find most painful when launching a data set.
Ask one domain team how long it took from idea to first consumer, and write the number down.

title: From empty folder to trusted product

beats.say: How does a team go from an empty folder to a trusted data product in days, not months?

show.sub: Empty folder to first consumer query

beats.say: It starts with a template repository. One click gives a contract file, a dbt project, tests, CI, and deployment. The contract names the schema, the owner, and a freshness target, say fifteen minutes.

Next, ingestion. Managed change data capture, which streams database changes, feeds lakehouse tables in a shared catalog. A schema registry rejects breaking changes. Each domain gets a quota, so one team cannot eat the whole warehouse.
On every run, contract checks and monitors fire. If freshness slips past fifteen minutes, the owner is paged. The catalog entry and lineage appear automatically from the contract and the jobs.

check.q: A table is two hours late, but the code passed CI. What catches this on the platform?
opts: A freshness monitor on each run that pages the product owner
The schema registry, which flags any table that arrives late
The catalog entry, which refreshes lineage and alerts consumers
The per-domain quota, which blocks slow jobs from running
check.why: CI tests code, not live data. Freshness monitors compare actual arrival against the contract target and page the owner. The registry, catalog and quotas do not measure lateness.

work: Write a freshness target into one contract and wire a monitor that pages a named owner.
Check that every template repo ships with tests and CI so nothing is added by hand.

title: Why the golden path still fails

beats.say: Your platform exists, so why are domains still filing tickets and going around it?

show.text: Platform built, yet tickets pile up

beats.say: First, template drift. A team copies the template once and never gets upgrades, so old products miss new checks. Fix it by versioning the template and sending automated pull requests when it changes.
Second, tag-based access only works if data is tagged. An untagged personal column slips past masking. So CI should fail any column that has no classification tag.
Third, checks in CI only test code, not data. Monitors must run on every run, or late, silent data reaches consumers. And a page needs an on-call rota, or it goes nowhere.

show.title: Close the gaps
items: CI tests code, not live data
Every page needs a named on-call

check.q: A new column holding customer emails reaches production unmasked. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The column had no classification tag, so no masking policy matched
The domain exceeded its compute quota, so masking was skipped
The schema registry rejected the change and left the old policy
The catalog lineage was stale, so audit logs were not written
check.why: Policy-based masking keys off tags and roles. An untagged column matches no policy. Quotas, the registry and lineage do not decide whether masking applies.

work: Add a CI rule that fails when any new column has no classification tag.
Count how many products still run an old template version and schedule upgrade pull requests.

title: When a platform is worth the cost

beats.say: When is a self-serve data platform a bad investment?

show.text: When is it a bad bet?

beats.say: With three domains and one data team, a central pipeline is cheaper. A platform team of eight engineers costs more than it saves until many domains are producing data. Below that, centralize and keep it simple.

Once it is worth it, run it as a product. Track days from new product to first consumer query, the share of products on the golden path, and how often domains ask for help. Rising help requests mean the path is too hard.

show.title: Platform metrics
items: Share of products on golden path

beats.say: Keep an escape hatch for unusual needs, but make it visible. And show cost per product each month, called showback, before any chargeback, so teams learn their bill without a fight.

check.q: Domain help requests to the platform team keep rising each month. What does this signal?
opts: The golden path is too hard or has gaps domains cannot self-serve
Domains are adopting the path well and asking for more features
The platform team needs stricter rules to stop outside tool use
Showback costs are too visible and are scaring teams into asking
check.why: Rising help requests mean the path is not truly self-serve. Fix the gaps rather than adding restrictions. Healthy adoption would show a rising path share and falling help requests.

work: Pull three platform metrics: days to first consumer query, golden path share, and help requests.
Estimate platform team cost against the number of domains it serves before approving headcount.

title: A data product is a shop with customers

beats.say: Would you open a bakery without knowing who will eat the bread?
A data product is the same. Before building, the team names its customers and the questions they want answered. Maybe finance wants last month's revenue by region. Write that down first.
After launch, count who actually shows up. How many people read it each week? How long does a newcomer take to get a first answer? How many questions do they have to ask?

show.title: Watch the shop
items: How long until a first answer

beats.say: And if nobody has bought the bread in three months, take it off the shelf. Say so first, wait, then remove it. Stale shelves make shoppers stop trusting the shop.

check.q: Why should a domain name its consumers before building a data product?
opts: So the product answers real questions that those people actually have
So the team can lock out anyone who was not named on the list
So the catalog has more entries to show during quarterly reviews
So the platform team can pick the storage format ahead of time
check.why: Product thinking starts from users and their questions, like user stories in an app team. Without that, you build tables nobody needs.

work: Write down the top three consumers and their questions for one dataset you own.
Ask a consumer what they tried first and where they got stuck.
List which tables in your area nobody has read lately.

title: Five numbers that show adoption

beats.say: You published a table. How do you know anyone cares?

Track five numbers. Weekly active consumers: distinct people or jobs reading it. Dependent products: other products built on top, which marks it as foundational. Time to first query: how long a new consumer takes to run a working query.
Add SLO attainment, the share of the last thirty days it met its freshness and quality promises. And support load: questions per week, and how many the docs should have answered.
Example: forty weekly consumers, six dependents, first query in two days. Healthy. Zero readers for ninety days? Announce, wait out the notice period, then archive.

check.q: What does a high count of dependent products tell you about a data product?
opts: Other products are built on it, so it is probably foundational
Its documentation is complete, so support questions should be zero
Its SLO is being met, so monitoring can safely be switched off
Its readers are unhappy, so the team should plan to retire it
check.why: Dependents are products built on top of it. Many of them means breaking changes will spread widely, so it needs care.

work: Add weekly active consumers and time to first query to your product dashboard.
Tag each support question as answered-by-docs or not, and count weekly.
Pick a deprecation trigger such as 90 days without readers.

title: Traps in adoption metrics

beats.say: Your product has forty weekly users. Is it a success?
Not necessarily. One scheduled job counts as one consumer, even if it feeds a hundred dashboards. Count dependent products too, or you will undervalue foundational data.
Beware vanity numbers. Many readers with a long time to first query means the docs are weak. High support load on questions the docs should answer is a documentation bug, not a user problem.

show.title: Read the numbers together
items: Many readers, slow first query: weak docs

beats.say: Deprecation has traps. Ninety days without readers can miss a quarterly or annual report job. Check lineage for dependents, announce to known consumers, wait out the notice period, then archive rather than delete, so you can restore it.

check.q: A product has had no reads for 90 days. What is the safest next step?
opts: Check lineage for rare jobs, announce, wait, then archive it
Delete it right away, since idle data only adds storage cost
Keep it forever, since removing anything breaks consumer trust
Rebuild it with a new schema so that readers will return soon
check.why: Quarterly or yearly jobs may not appear in a 90-day window. Announce, wait for the notice period, and archive so it can be restored.

work: Join read logs with lineage so scheduled jobs show their downstream users.
Review the last 30 support questions and fix the docs behind repeated ones.
Check that deprecation windows cover quarterly and annual reporting jobs.

title: When product thinking is not worth it

beats.say: Should every dataset become a data product?
No. Product thinking costs a named owner, documentation, an SLO and on-call time. For a table with one reader, a shared team table is cheaper and honest.
Spend the effort where adoption proves it pays: high weekly consumers, many dependents. Those earn strict contracts and tight SLOs. Low adoption earns lighter support or retirement.

Make retirement automatic. The platform should publish these metrics, flag products with ninety idle days, and start the notice. Otherwise the catalog fills with dead tables, and people stop trusting it, then build private copies.

check.q: How should an architect decide how much product rigor a dataset gets?
opts: Match rigor to adoption, with strict SLOs only where use is high
Give every dataset the same rigor so that the catalog is uniform
Give rigor only to the newest datasets, as older ones are stable
Give rigor by table size, since large tables cost the most to run
check.why: Owners, docs and SLOs cost real time. Adoption shows where that cost pays off, and low-use products should be simplified or retired.

work: Define tiers such as foundational, standard and retire, with adoption thresholds.
Have the platform flag 90-day idle products and send notices automatically.
Review the catalog quarterly and retire what has no consumers.

title: The kitchen that cannot close overnight

beats.say: Imagine one giant kitchen cooks every meal for a whole city. Orders pile up. Could you hand kitchens to each neighbourhood overnight?
No. First you build shared equipment: standard recipes, health checks, and a price tag per dish. That is the platform. The old kitchen uses it first.
Then try two or three neighbourhoods that have real cooks and real customers. Cooks from the central kitchen move over to help.
Run old and new side by side until the meals taste the same. Then move customers over. Other neighbourhoods join when they ask to.

check.q: Why does the central kitchen build shared equipment before any neighbourhood takes over?
opts: Every new kitchen needs the same tools and rules, or quality varies
Shared equipment lets the central kitchen cook more meals faster
Neighbourhoods are not allowed to buy their own equipment
Building tools first means no pilots are needed afterwards
check.why: Without a common platform, each domain would invent its own checks and standards, so quality and cost would vary wildly. The platform is what makes handing over ownership safe.

work: List which tools a new team would need to publish a dataset safely, and see how many already exist.
Ask which team has real consumers and engineers, and could be a first pilot.

title: The five-step migration sequence

beats.say: How do you move a hundred tables from a central warehouse team to domain owners without breaking a single dashboard?

show.sub: Order of steps is the whole trick

beats.say: Build the platform first: contract files, automated checks in the build pipeline, a catalog, SLO monitors, and cost per product. The central team uses it on its own tables before any domain does.
Pick two or three lighthouse domains with engineers, a business owner and real consumers. The source team signs a contract for what it emits, so central pipelines stop breaking on surprise changes.
Then dual run. The old table and the new product run together for, say, four weeks, until counts and totals match. Move consumers in groups, then deprecate the old table.

check.q: What must be in place before ownership of a table moves to a domain team?
opts: A signed contract for what the source emits, plus platform tooling
A promise from the domain to fix breaks within one working day
A full rewrite of every consumer to read the new product
Approval from leadership to close the central team down
check.why: Contracts at the boundary stop upstream changes from breaking central pipelines, and the platform gives the domain the checks it needs. Promises, rewrites and closures do not protect consumers.

work: Pick one table with frequent upstream breaks and draft a contract for it.
Define a reconciliation query that compares row counts and key totals between old and new.

title: Why migrations stall after the pilot

beats.say: Why do so many mesh migrations stall right after the pilot looks successful?
Trap one: ownership moved before contracts. The domain renames a column, and a central pipeline that still reads it fails at three in the morning. So contracts come first, signed by the source team.
Trap two: reconciliation. Numbers rarely match exactly, because of time zones, late events and rounding. Agree a tolerance, such as under 0.1 percent, and explain every gap before cutover.
Trap three: never switching off the old table. Then two versions of the truth live forever. Set a date, warn consumers, and delete it.

show.title: Finish the job
items: Track who still reads the old table

check.q: Old and new tables differ by a small amount during dual run. What is the right response?
opts: Find the cause of each gap and agree a tolerance before cutover
Cut over anyway because small gaps are always rounding noise
Extend dual run indefinitely until both match to the last cent
Trust the old table and drop the new product from the plan
check.why: Gaps usually come from time zones, late events or rounding. Explaining them and agreeing a tolerance builds trust. Ignoring them is risky, and waiting for a perfect match stops the migration.

work: Write down the tolerance and the known reasons for gaps before the next dual run starts.
Put a deprecation date and a read-access report on every old table in scope.

title: When mesh migration is the wrong call

beats.say: When should you decide not to migrate to mesh at all?
If you have few domains, little engineering talent inside them, or a central team that clears its backlog quickly, mesh adds duplicate work and platform cost. A good central team can beat it.

If you proceed, grow by demand. Mandates create domains with no engineers and poorly owned products. Keep shared aggregates, like company revenue, central, because no single domain owns that definition.
Prove it with numbers leadership understands: backlog length, incidents from upstream changes, time to ship a dataset, and share of consumers reading certified products. If they do not move, stop.

show.title: Migration scorecard
items: Time to ship a new dataset
Share of consumers on certified products

check.q: What is the best signal that a new domain is ready to take ownership?
opts: The domain asks to join because the golden path saves it time
The central team announces a date by which all domains must move
The domain has the largest tables in the warehouse
The domain has agreed to share its cloud budget with the platform
check.why: Pull from demand means the platform is good enough that domains choose it, and they bring engineers and owners. Mandates and table size say nothing about readiness.

work: Baseline the four scorecard numbers today so you can show movement later.
List which aggregate products must stay central, and name the owner for each.

title: A city with a few shared rules

beats.say: How do you keep company data tidy when every team builds its own?

Picture a city of neighborhoods. Each one builds houses its own way. But the whole city agrees on a few rules, like street names and fire exits. A council with one person from each neighborhood agrees them. That is what federated means.

Now the clever part. The city sends no inspector to knock on doors. Instead the permit machine refuses any plan without a fire exit. Rules checked by the system itself are called computational governance. Nobody waits for a meeting.
Everything else, like paint colour, stays the neighborhood's choice.

show.title: Global versus local
items: Global: a few rules, checked by code

check.q: What makes governance in a data mesh computational?
opts: The platform enforces the rules automatically with code
The rules are written down in a long shared policy document
A central team reviews every dataset by hand each week
Each domain decides for itself which rules it will follow
check.why: Computational means the platform checks and enforces rules in code, so nobody waits for a meeting. Documents, manual review and optional rules all depend on people remembering.

work: List the rules your company says it has, and mark which ones a program could check.
Ask who sits on your data council and whether every domain has a seat.
Pick one rule that is only enforced by meetings and sketch how code could check it.

title: The publish gate, step by step

beats.say: What actually happens when a team tries to publish a data product?

The platform runs a gate in the publishing pipeline. It reads the product's metadata and checks a handful of rules. Is there an owner? A contract? A freshness target, say data under 1 hour old, and a completeness target, say 99 percent of rows present? Miss one, and the publish fails with a clear message.

Privacy works the same way. Columns tagged as personal, like email, are masked at query time unless the reader's role allows it. Naming and shared keys such as customer id are linted too, so products can join.
Retention runs on a schedule by data class, and a breaking change must be a new major version with 90 days notice.

show.title: Automatic rules
items: Breaking change means new major version

check.q: A product has no freshness SLO in its metadata. What should the platform do?
opts: Block the publish and tell the owner which rule failed
Publish it now and ask the team to add one later
Pick a default SLO and publish without telling anyone
Send the spec to the council for a manual decision
check.why: The gate exists so every published product meets the global rules. Publishing anyway, silent defaults or manual review each bring back gaps or meetings.

work: Write the publish checklist as a small automated test that reads product metadata.
Tag personal columns in one product and confirm masking changes by role.
Add a check that rejects a schema change without a new major version.

title: Why a passing product can drift

beats.say: Your product passed every check at publish. So why is it breaking the rules today?

show.text: Passed on day one. Broken today?

beats.say: Because a gate only checks one moment. Data drifts. Someone adds a column called phone, forgets the personal tag, and it is served unmasked. So good platforms also scan continuously and flag untagged columns that look like personal data.

chip.text: Scan continuously, not just at publish

beats.say: Second trap: a declared SLO is only a promise. Governance must measure it, and alert the owner when freshness slips past the target. And a schema diff catches a dropped column, but not a column whose meaning quietly changed, such as price switching from euros to cents.
Finally, new rules hit old products. Roll them out as warnings first, then enforce after a grace period, or you block every team on day one.

check.q: A product passed the publish gate months ago. What is the main risk if governance only checks at publish?
opts: Later changes can break the rules and nobody notices
The gate will run too slowly for large products
Old products will be deleted by the retention rule
Consumers will be unable to join on shared keys
check.why: A publish gate sees a single moment, so untagged columns, missed SLOs and changed meaning can appear afterwards. Continuous scanning and SLO monitoring close that gap.

work: Add a scheduled scan that flags columns named like personal data but lacking a tag.
Measure each product's freshness against its SLO and alert the owner on breach.
Introduce your next rule in warn mode for a few weeks before you enforce it.

title: When this model is the wrong call

beats.say: When is federated computational governance the wrong choice?

show.text: When is it the wrong choice?

beats.say: When you are small. With two or three data teams, a central team and a shared warehouse are cheaper. Building policy engines, catalogs and checks takes a platform team, often five or more engineers, and that cost only pays off when many domains publish.

The design test for each rule: can code check it? If not, ask whether it is worth having. Every global rule also taxes every team, so keep the list near six, and let domains choose tools and modelling.
Watch the council too. If it becomes an approval queue, you have rebuilt the central bottleneck. Its job is to change rules, review exceptions and track pass rates.

check.q: A company has three data teams and one shared warehouse. What is the best governance choice?
opts: Keep central governance and revisit when domains multiply
Build a full policy platform now to be ready for growth
Let every team set its own rules to move quickly
Form a council that approves every dataset by hand
check.why: Computational governance needs a platform team whose cost pays off only with many publishing domains. At small scale a central team is cheaper, while manual approval just recreates a bottleneck.

work: Count your publishing domains and estimate platform effort before proposing a mesh.
Review each global rule and remove any that nobody can check automatically.
Track council decisions and make sure it spends time on rules and exceptions, not approvals.

title: Food court with no manager

beats.say: What happens when a company gives every team its own data, but no tools and no rules?
Picture a food court. Each stall owns its menu, its cooks and its cleaning. That is a data mesh. Each business area owns its data and treats it like a product.

Now it goes wrong. A stall changes its sign, but the same boss runs it. That is mesh-washing. Three stalls sell a dish called customer, with different prices. Those are duplicate products. A stall closes and nobody cleans its fridge. That is an orphaned product.
The fix is simple. Real owners, one shared kitchen, a few rules, and a name on every stall.

check.q: A warehouse team is renamed the Data Domain team, and nothing else changes. What is this?
opts: Mesh-washing, because ownership, budget and on-call never moved
A healthy first step, because renaming creates real ownership
A platform gap, because the shared tools are missing
Governance theatre, because too many review boards exist
check.why: Mesh-washing is a label change. A mesh is real only when ownership, budget and on-call duty move to the domains.

work: List your data products and write the owning team beside each one.
Check whether any domain team actually carries the on-call pager for its data.

title: Stopping the three customer tables

beats.say: Twelve domains can publish data. Six months later there are three customer tables with three different counts. How do you stop that?
First, a global identifier. Every customer gets one key, used by all products. Before publishing, a team searches the catalog. If customer exists, they extend it. One concept, one owner.
Second, a platform. Instead of twelve teams building twelve Kafka clusters, the platform offers a golden path. That is a template creating a pipeline, storage and alerts in about an hour.
Third, rules enforced in code. The publish step fails if the owner field is empty or the timestamp is not in UTC. No meeting needed.

show.title: Publish check
show.text:
owner is set
timestamp is UTC
customer_id present
else: block publish

check.q: Why does a golden path reduce failure across twelve domains?
opts: It gives every team the same ready-made pipeline, storage and alerts
It forces all twelve domains to share one single data owner
It replaces the catalog so teams no longer search before publishing
It lets each domain choose its own tools without any limits
check.why: A golden path is a shared template. Teams get working infrastructure fast, so they do not each build and run their own.

work: Pick one rule, such as owner required, and make the publish pipeline reject products without it.
Add a catalog search step to your publishing checklist.

title: Slides good, data broken

beats.say: Why do mesh programs with great slides still produce broken data?

Often domains lack data skills. A sales team owns a product, but nobody can fix a late pipeline at two in the morning. Embed data engineers in the domain, and use an enabling team that coaches rather than does the work.
Governance theatre is another trap. A review board meets every two weeks, approves things, and nobody checks them later. Keep about five rules, and test each one automatically.

show.title: Governance that works
items: Tested in code on every publish
No board in the critical path

beats.say: Then interoperability. If orders use local time, payments use UTC, and currencies are mixed, a join silently gives wrong totals. Make keys, time zones and currencies global rules.

check.q: A review board approves every product, but nobody checks them afterwards. What is the best fix?
opts: Enforce a few rules automatically in the publishing pipeline
Add a second review board to double-check the first one
Write a longer policy document covering every edge case
Ask each domain to promise it follows the rules
check.why: Rules that run in code are checked every time. Meetings and promises decay, so governance theatre fades only when checks are automated.

work: Count your governance rules and delete any that nothing actually checks.
Audit two products you join often for key, time zone and currency mismatches.

title: When the mesh gets expensive

beats.say: Your mesh works, then the cloud bill triples. What happened?
Every domain started its own cluster running around the clock. Ten small clusters idle at night still cost every hour. Use shared compute with quotas, and show each team the cost per product.

Orphans are the quiet cost. A team reorganises, the product stays live, and nobody answers when it breaks. Make ownership a team, not a person. Move it on reorganisation, and block publication without an owner.
And know when not to do this. With three domains and one small data team, a central warehouse is cheaper and simpler. Mesh pays off when the central team becomes the bottleneck.

show.title: Choose by scale
items: Either way: owners and cost visibility

check.q: A company has three domains and one small data team. What is the sensible choice?
opts: Keep a central warehouse, since mesh overhead outweighs its benefit here
Adopt a full mesh, since ownership should always be distributed
Give each domain its own cluster, since isolation prevents cost problems
Skip ownership rules, since small teams never create orphans
check.why: Mesh adds platform, governance and coordination cost. It pays off when a central team is the bottleneck, not at small scale.

work: Show each team its monthly compute cost per data product.
Set quotas on shared compute before giving domains their own clusters.
Assign every product to a team and transfer it during reorganisations.
